title: Why Do NPS and Support Ticket Trends Disagree, and Which One Should You Trust?
summary: NPS and support tickets sample different customers, so disagreement is information. Four checks to run, and which signal to act on first.
body_markdown:
Your net promoter score (NPS) is up four points this quarter. Support tickets are up eleven percent. One dashboard says customers are happier. The other says more of them are in trouble. Someone on the executive team wants to know which number is real before the quarterly review.


Both are real. They disagree because they describe different people. NPS describes customers who were sampled, reached, and chose to answer. The ticket trend describes customers who hit a problem and chose to contact you. A gap between two populations assembled that differently is the normal case, not a data quality failure.


So the question isn't which number to believe. It's which of four things the gap represents: a real change in experience, a denominator change, a survey instrument change, or a cohort mismatch. Thematic combines survey responses and support conversations into a Lens, which analyzes them under a single, unified set of themes, so the two can be compared theme by theme instead of headline by headline. Below are the four checks, and a rule for which signal to act on first.


## Why the two signals disagree by construction


A survey trend and a ticket trend sample different populations on purpose.


Surveys reach people you selected who then opted in. Tickets reach you from people who hit enough friction to make contact worth the effort, and who believed contacting you would help. Neither group is the customer base. One metropolitan water utility found that only 15% of its customer base proactively contacts it in a typical month, leaving 85% of its customers invisible to the contact channel entirely.


This is also why your survey response rate settles nothing.[Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/05/RDD-Non-response-Full-Report.pdf) concludes plainly that "response rate is an unreliable indicator of bias." There's a fuller argument elsewhere on this blog for why a response rate[can't prove representativeness](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-representative-not-loudest-customers) . Here the point is narrower: both lines are partial views, and the disagreement between them is where the information is.


## Four things a disagreement can mean


Before you tell an executive that customer experience improved or deteriorated, work through four possibilities. Three of them are boring.


- **A denominator change.** Ticket volume rose because you have more customers, more orders, or a longer reporting window, not because anything got worse.
- **An instrument change.** The survey wording, the trigger timing, or the channel changed between periods, so the score moved without customers moving.
- **A cohort mismatch.** The two signals are reading different segments, different products, or different time windows, so they were never comparable.
- **A real change in experience.** What's left after you've eliminated the other three.


Only the fourth one is news. The first three are measurement artifacts, and they're more common than most dashboards admit.


## Check 1: Is the ticket line a volume change or a rate change?


Convert the ticket count to a rate before you interpret it.


Epidemiology states the principle most cleanly. As the[CDC's own epidemiology curriculum](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/section1.html) puts it, "rates put disease frequency in the perspective of the size of the population." A count tells you how much work arrived. A rate tells you whether customers are hitting problems more often. Tickets per thousand active customers, per thousand orders, or per thousand sessions are often flat in a quarter where the raw count climbed.


Don't chase an external benchmark here. There's no credible cross-industry figure for tickets per customer. Every number in circulation traces back to a vendor calculator or an unsourced statistics page, so your only honest comparison is your own trailing baseline.


Volume still matters on its own terms, because in a support queue every contact is a real event someone had to handle. Within a Lens, Thematic can use volume itself as the score for that reason, measuring a theme by how many responses it drives rather than by how people rated it. That gives a ticket feed a comparable measure even though no survey score is attached to it.


## Check 2: Did the survey instrument change?


If anything about the survey changed between periods,[the trend line is the suspect](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-feedback-trend-lines-comparable) , not the customers.


The published evidence is larger than most CX teams expect. In[one Pew experiment](https://www.pewresearch.org/writing-survey-questions/) , changing only the question that came before a satisfaction item moved the result 10 points, from 78% to 88% dissatisfied.[Changing the channel alone](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2015/05/14/where-web-surveys-produce-different-results-than-phone-interviews/) has a comparable effect: 62% of phone respondents said they were "very satisfied" with their family life, against 44% of web respondents answering the same question.


One finding matters more than the rest for NPS.[Pew reports](https://www.pewresearch.org/methods/2019/02/27/what-our-transition-to-online-polling-means-for-decades-of-phone-survey-trends/) that on rating scales, "telephone poll respondents are more likely than online survey respondents to select extremely positive answers but are not more likely to give extremely negative responses." NPS is an eleven-point rating scale whose result depends on the top two boxes. A change in survey mode can move your promoter count without touching your detractor count, which looks exactly like a genuine improvement.


Pew's guidance is that comparing to earlier surveys requires identical question wording and similar question context. When that isn't true, its documented practice is blunt: "'Breaking the trend' may break a researcher's heart, but in these cases the Center will drop the prior years' data and present only the new online estimates." Telling an executive that this quarter isn't comparable to last quarter is a defensible answer, and often the correct one.


## Check 3: Are the two signals reading the same cohort?


Line the two signals up on the same population and the same clock before concluding anything.


Three mismatches do most of the damage. **Segment:** a relationship survey fielded across the whole base won't track a ticket trend concentrated in one product line. **Timing:** a customer who contacts support in March may not be surveyed until June, so the two lines move in different months for the same event. **Window:** several[helpdesk analytics features](https://getthematic.com/insights/helpdesk-ai-ticket-volume-drivers) look back only 90 days and can't show you a year.


A quieter mismatch sits inside the survey data. Thematic's Impact score is calculated by default from responses that have both a score and a written comment, so it describes the people who scored you and said why. That's a narrower group than everyone who contacted you, and it's worth saying out loud when the two analyses sit side by side.


## Check 4: Do the two signals agree at the theme level?


Headline numbers can't disagree usefully. Themes can.


Run the same theme set across both sources and compare the ranking. When you add a new data source to an existing Lens in Thematic, it automatically picks up that Lens's themes, so surveys and support conversations are coded the same way rather than in two separate taxonomies. Thematic pulls support conversations straight from Zendesk and Intercom, so the comparison is a filter change rather than an integration project. In the Comparison tool you apply a primary filter and an orange "Compare with" filter to put two segments side by side. Hovering a theme shows whether the volume difference between them is statistically significant.


You're looking for a theme that's large in one source and small in the other. At a US online lending marketplace working through more than 20,000 customer comments every 90 days, a "Timing of Call" theme turned out to be disproportionately[driving detractors in NPS surveys](https://getthematic.com/insights/find-what-is-driving-nps-score) . Leads were being called outside normal hours across US time zones. That's an operational, contact-side cause surfacing in survey data. It runs in reverse too, which is why[a theme climbing in tickets](https://getthematic.com/insights/spot-emerging-support-issues-customer-feedback) while the survey stays flat deserves attention rather than dismissal.


## Which one should you trust?


Trust the ticket trend first when you need to act, and the survey trend when you need to report.


Tickets are closer to a leading indicator, surveys closer to a lagging one. Outside CX[the distinction is standard](https://ccohs.ca/oshanswers/hsprograms/leading-and-lagging-indicators.html) : lagging indicators are "a record of what has happened" and "do not reveal whether an organization will be effective at preventing incidents," while leading indicators are "proactive, preventative, and predictive." A theme rising in your support queue is a problem happening now. A score that moved is a verdict on a quarter that already closed.


Practitioners make this trade explicitly. Anastasia Zdoroviak, Senior Manager of Customer Experience at DoorDash,[told Forrester analyst Angelina Gennis](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/get-smart-on-cx-teams-an-interview-with-doordash/) : "We knew \[the\] Net Promoter Score (NPS) wasn't the right metric to indicate improvement, so we tracked number of support interactions and observed that fewer candidates dropped during the application process."


That's not an argument for abandoning NPS. A[meta-analysis covering 1,160,982 people](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11002-023-09671-w) found satisfaction positively associated with customer and firm outcomes, with the strength varying by how it was measured. How you measure changes what you find. That's the case for reading both lines together.


## What to ask before your next executive review


1. Have we converted ticket counts to a rate against active customers, orders, or sessions?
2. Did the survey wording, trigger timing, or channel change between the two periods?
3. Are both signals filtered to the same segment, product line, and date range?
4. Is the survey move larger than the sampling noise for our response volume?
5. Do the top five themes rank the same way in both sources over the same period?
6. If the instrument changed, are we prepared to say the periods aren't comparable?


## The short answer


NPS and support ticket trends disagree because they sample different customers and measure different things, so the disagreement is usually information rather than error. Rule out a denominator change, an instrument change, and a cohort mismatch before you call it a real change in experience. Then act on the ticket trend, which tells you what's happening now. Report on the survey trend, which tells you what it cost.


The test to run this week: take your top five themes from survey verbatims, measure the same five across your support conversations for the same period and segment, and see which change rank. Those are where your two dashboards stopped agreeing.
